lessons.title: Identifying Shock Absorbers, Struts, and Control Arms
lessons.body: Shock absorbers and struts control your vehicle's bounce and keep tyres on the road. In Africa, rough roads destroy them fast. A worn shock leaks oil, causing the car to float and stop poorly. Park on flat ground and push down hard on one corner of the bumper. If it bounces more than twice, the shock is weak. Look behind each wheel: a good shock is dry; a bad one has oil streaks. Struts are shocks inside a coil spring, common on front-wheel-drive cars like Toyota Corolla or Nissan Sunny. They are thicker and have a spring seat. Control arms connect the wheel hub to the frame, with bushings and a ball joint. Worn control arm bushings cause clunks over bumps. Check by rocking the wheel top-to-bottom; if there's play, the ball joint or bushing is bad. Tools: jack, jack stands, 17mm and 19mm spanners, pry bar. On a Toyota Hilux, rear shocks are eye-to-eye; front struts need a spring compressor. In scrap yards, match part numbers stamped on the shock body. Never buy a used shock that's wet with oil. For control arms, inspect the bushing for cracks and the ball joint for looseness. African roads mean check every 20,000 km or after any big pothole hit. Replace in pairs (both front or both rear) to keep balance. Torque bolts with the suspension loaded (car on ground) to avoid bushing twist. If you hear a knock when turning, it's often a strut mount bearing. Identifying these parts correctly saves money and prevents accidents.

lessons.title: Replacing Worn Suspension Bushings
lessons.body: Suspension bushings are rubber or polyurethane cushions that isolate noise and allow movement. When they crack or squash, you get clunks, vague steering, and uneven tyre wear. Common locations: control arms, sway bar, and trailing arms. On African roads, heat and dust make rubber brittle. To check, park on flat ground and use a pry bar to wiggle the arm; if the bushing moves more than 2mm, replace it. Tools: jack, stands, 14mm-19mm spanners, socket set, hammer, chisel, and a bush press or large vice. For a Toyota Corolla front control arm bushing: raise and support the car, remove the wheel, unbolt the control arm (two bolts to frame, one to ball joint). Take the arm to a workbench. Use a hammer and chisel to cut out the old rubber, then hacksaw the metal sleeve and punch it out. Clean the bore. Press in the new bushing with a vice and suitable socketsâlubricate with soapy water, not oil. Polyurethane bushings last longer but squeak; use silicone grease. Refit the arm, hand-tighten bolts, lower the car, then torque to 80-100 Nm with the suspension loaded. For sway bar bushings, it's easier: unbolt the bracket, slide off old bushings, slide on new ones, and rebolt. Test drive over speed bumps; clunks should be gone. In Africa, buy bushings from a trusted parts shop; cheap ones fail in months. Replace in pairs. If you lack a press, many garages will press them for a small fee. Always check alignment after.

lessons.title: Checking and Replacing Tie Rod Ends
lessons.body: Tie rod ends connect the steering rack to the wheel hub. Worn ends cause vague steering, shimmy, and uneven tyre wear. In Africa, potholes and dust accelerate wear. To check: raise the front of the car on jack stands. Grab the front tyre at 3 and 9 o'clock and wiggle. If you feel play, look at the tie rod endâif it moves independently of the steering arm, it's worn. Also check the rubber boot; if torn, grease escapes and dirt enters. Another test: with the car on the ground, have a helper turn the steering wheel slightly left and right while you watch the tie rod. Any delay or clunk means replacement. Tools: 17mm, 19mm spanners, ball joint separator (pickle fork), hammer, pliers, and a torque wrench. For a Nissan Note: loosen the lock nut on the tie rod (use 22mm). Remove the cotter pin and castle nut (19mm) from the tie rod end. Use a pickle fork or hit the steering arm with a hammer to pop it out. Unscrew the old end, counting turns to keep alignment close. Screw on the new end the same number of turns. Tighten the castle nut to 40-50 Nm and fit a new cotter pin. Tighten the lock nut. Do both sides if one is worn. After replacement, you must align the steering. In Africa, buy tie rod ends from reputable brands; cheap ones fail quickly. Test drive: steering should be firm, no shimmy. If the steering wheel is off-centre, adjust the tie rods equally. Always replace in pairs.

lessons.title: Aligning Steering After Suspension Work
lessons.body: After replacing suspension or steering parts, your wheel alignment is off. Misalignment causes rapid tyre wear, pulling, and poor fuel economy. In Africa, where tyres are expensive, alignment saves money. You need a flat, level surface and basic tools: two long strings, jack stands, a measuring tape, and a 19mm spanner. First, set the steering wheel straight. Check toe: measure the distance between the front of the front tyres and the rear of the front tyres at hub height. The front should be 0 to 3mm less than the rear (toe-in). If not, adjust the tie rods. Loosen the lock nuts and turn the tie rod with a 22mm spanner. Turning the rod one flat changes toe by about 1mm. Adjust both sides equally to keep the steering wheel centred. For camber and caster, you need a proper alignment shopâbut after basic suspension work, toe is the main concern. On a Toyota Hilux, toe-in spec is 0 to 2mm. Test drive on a straight road: the steering wheel should be centred and the car should not pull. If it pulls, check tyre pressures first. In Africa, many garages offer alignment for a small fee; but you can do a string alignment: run a string parallel to the rear wheel and measure the gap to the front wheel. Adjust until equal. Always align after replacing tie rod ends, control arms, or struts. Recheck after 100 km. Proper alignment extends tyre life by thousands of kilometres.

lessons.title: Diagnosing Uneven Tyre Wear
lessons.body: Uneven tyre wear tells you what's wrong with your suspension and steering. In Africa, where roads are rough and tyres costly, reading wear patterns saves money. First, check tyre pressure monthlyâwrong pressure causes centre or edge wear. If the centre is worn, pressure is too high; edges worn, too low. Next, look at the pattern. Wear on one side of the tread (inner or outer) means camber is offâoften from worn ball joints or bent struts. Feathered edges (scooped) indicate toe misalignment; the tyre scrubs sideways. Cupped or scalloped wear (dips around the tread) points to worn shocks or strutsâthe tyre bounces and skips. If you see a single bald spot, it's a locked brake or a flat spot from skidding. To diagnose: park on flat ground, turn the steering fully left, and inspect the inner edge of the right tyre; then turn right and check the left. Use a tread depth gauge (or a coin) to measure across the tread. If the difference is more than 1.5mm, you have a problem. Check for play in tie rods, ball joints, and wheel bearings. For example, on a Toyota Corolla, inner edge wear on both front tyres usually means too much negative camber from worn struts or control arm bushings. Fix the worn parts, then get an alignment. Rotate tyres every 5,000 km to even out wear. In Africa, buy quality tyres and keep them inflated. If you catch wear early, you can save the tyre; if cords show, replace immediately.

lessons.title: Sourcing Used Suspension Parts from Scrap Yards
lessons.body: Scrap yards (also called breakers or dumps) are gold mines for used suspension parts in Africa. You can save 50-70% compared to new, but you must inspect carefully. Common parts: shocks, struts, control arms, tie rods, and bushings. Start by knowing your car's make, model, year, and engine size. Bring a torch, a pry bar, a 17mm and 19mm spanner, and a rag. At the yard, look for a car that was rear-ended or rolledâsuspension parts are often still good. Avoid cars with front-end damage if you need front suspension. For shocks: check for oil leaks, rust, and smooth operation. Push the rod in and out; it should resist evenly and rebound once. If it's easy or jerky, reject. For struts: check the spring for cracks and the mount bearing for roughness. For control arms: inspect bushings for cracks and ball joint for playâwiggle the stud. For tie rod ends: the ball should be tight but movable; boot intact. Never buy a part that looks freshly paintedâit may hide damage. Ask the yard owner if you can return it if it doesn't fit. In Africa, many yards let you test-fit on your car in the yard. Price guide: used shock $10-20, control arm $15-30, tie rod end $5-10. Always replace bushings and boots on used parts. Clean and paint them before fitting. If you buy a used strut, consider replacing the shock cartridge inside. Bargain hardâyards expect it. Take photos of your old part to match. If you're unsure, bring a mechanic friend. A good used part can last years; a bad one can cause an accident.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Suspension and Steering Parts

In African auto repair and parts businesses, suspension and steering work is one of the most reliable income streams. Vehicles operate on rough roads, overloaded routes, and long-distance corridors where shocks, bushings, and tie rod ends wear out faster than in Europe or Asia. For a workshop owner, parts reseller, or roadside mechanic, mastering suspension and steering diagnostics and replacement is not just a technical skill â it is a business advantage. This reference module gives you the practical knowledge to inspect, replace, and source components efficiently, reduce comebacks, and price jobs correctly.

This lesson covers shock absorbers, struts, control arms, bushings, tie rod ends, steering alignment, uneven tyre wear diagnosis, and sourcing used parts from scrap yards. Each section is written for the African context: limited diagnostic equipment, mixed vehicle fleets (Toyota, Nissan, Isuzu, Mitsubishi, Hyundai, Kia, and Chinese brands), and the reality that many customers buy used parts. Your goal is to deliver safe, roadworthy repairs while protecting your reputation and margin.

Identifying Shock Absorbers, Struts, and Control Arms

Shock absorbers control spring oscillation and keep tyres in contact with the road. Struts combine the shock absorber with the coil spring and structural support, common on front suspensions of Toyota Corolla, Nissan Almera, and most small sedans. Control arms connect the chassis to the wheel hub and carry the ball joint. In African workshops, the quickest identification method is visual and tactile: check for oil leakage on the shock body, bounce the corner of the vehicle (more than two rebounds means worn shocks), and inspect control arm bushings for cracks or separation. A worn control arm often causes clunking over bumps and uneven tyre wear.

For business purposes, stock fast-moving struts and shocks for Toyota Hilux, Nissan NP200, Isuzu D-Max, and Toyota Quantum â these are the backbone of African transport fleets. Buy in pairs and always quote the customer for both sides to avoid premature comebacks.

Replacing Worn Suspension Bushings

Bushings are cheap parts that cause expensive problems if ignored. Worn control arm bushings, sway bar bushings, and trailing arm bushings lead to vague steering, uneven tyre wear, and noise. In many African markets, polyurethane bushings are preferred for durability on rough roads, though rubber bushings give a softer ride. Replacement requires a press or a bushing removal tool. If you lack a hydraulic press, many workshops use a heavy vice and correctly sized sockets â but this risks damaging the arm. Invest in a press if you do suspension work weekly; it pays for itself within a few jobs.

Labour time: 1â2 hours per arm depending on corrosion. In coastal cities like Mombasa, Dar es Salaam, or Lagos, rust makes this job harder. Charge accordingly and use penetrating oil overnight.

Checking and Replacing Tie Rod Ends

Tie rod ends transfer steering input from the rack to the wheel hub. Worn tie rod ends cause steering play, uneven tyre wear, and can fail completely. The check is simple: raise the front of the vehicle, grab the wheel at 3 and 9 o'clock, and rock it. If there is movement before the steering wheel moves, the tie rod end or rack is worn. Also inspect the rubber boot for tears and grease loss. Replace inner and outer tie rod ends as a set where possible, and always perform a wheel alignment afterward.

In the African aftermarket, tie rod ends for Toyota, Nissan, and Isuzu are widely available from brands like CTR, Sankei, and 555. Avoid unbranded parts for safety-critical steering components â a failed tie rod end can cause a fatal accident and destroy your business reputation.

Aligning Steering After Suspension Work

Any suspension or steering replacement â struts, control arms, tie rod ends, or bushings â changes the wheel alignment geometry. Driving without alignment causes rapid tyre wear, poor handling, and increased fuel consumption. In Africa, many small workshops do not have laser alignment equipment. The minimum acceptable practice is a string alignment or a manual camber/caster gauge. If you cannot align in-house, partner with a tyre shop that has alignment equipment and include the cost in your quote.

Toe settings are the most critical for tyre wear. Toe-in or toe-out beyond specification will scrub tyres bald within a few thousand kilometres. Always test-drive after alignment and check the steering wheel is centred.

Diagnosing Uneven Tyre Wear

Uneven tyre wear is a diagnostic goldmine. It tells you what is wrong before you even lift the vehicle. Use the table below to match wear patterns to causes.

Table 1: Tyre wear patterns and likely suspension/steering causes
Wear Pattern Likely Cause Action
Wear on both inner and outer edges Under-inflation or worn shocks Check tyre pressure; replace shocks
Wear on one inner or outer edge Incorrect camber or toe Wheel alignment; inspect control arms
Feathered or scalloped tread Worn tie rod ends or bushings Replace tie rod ends; align
Cupping (dips in tread) Worn shocks or struts Replace shocks/struts in pairs
Centre wear Over-inflation Adjust tyre pressure
Diagonal wear or flat spots Worn bushings or bent components Inspect and replace worn parts

Source: Adapted from TyreSafe tyre wear guidance and Bridgestone tyre care resources.

Sourcing Used Suspension Parts from Scrap Yards

Used parts are a major part of the African auto market. A well-chosen used strut or control arm can save a customer 50â70% of new part cost. But your business depends on quality control. Never fit a used shock absorber that shows oil leakage. Never fit a used tie rod end with a torn boot or play. For control arms, check the bushing and ball joint condition â if the ball joint is loose, the arm is scrap.

Build relationships with 2â3 reputable scrap yards. Pay for parts you can inspect, and keep a warranty policy of 7â14 days for used suspension parts. Document the vehicle make, model, and year the part came from. This protects you if the customer returns with a complaint.

Table 2: New vs used suspension parts â business decision guide
Part New Part Cost (typical African market) Used Part Cost Recommendation
Shock absorber (Toyota Hilux front) USD 45â90 USD 15â30 New preferred; used only if leak-free and tested
Strut assembly (Nissan Almera) USD 70â140 USD 25â50 New preferred for safety; used risky
Control arm (Isuzu D-Max) USD 50â120 USD 20â45 Used acceptable if ball joint and bushings good
Tie rod end (Toyota Corolla) USD 12â25 USD 5â10 Always new â safety-critical
Suspension bushing set USD 10â30 USD 4â12 New preferred; used bushings often already worn

Source: Indicative pricing based on AutoZone and RockAuto catalogue ranges, adjusted for African import and local market conditions. Actual prices vary by country and supplier.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Suspension and Steering

Suspension and steering components are safety-critical. Never fit used tie rod ends, ball joints, or steering racks. Never reuse a strut with a bent piston rod or a shock absorber with oil leakage. Always use spring compressors correctly when working on struts â a released coil spring can cause fatal injury. Always torque fasteners to manufacturer specification and perform a wheel alignment after any steering or suspension replacement. Test-drive the vehicle at low speed before returning it to the customer. If you are unsure, stop and consult a qualified mechanic. A failed suspension part at speed can kill.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Inspect before quoting: Bounce test, visual leak check, and tyre wear pattern analysis before giving a price.
  • Replace in pairs: Shocks, struts, and tie rod ends should be replaced on both sides of an axle.
  • Check related parts: When replacing a control arm, inspect ball joint, bushings, and tie rod ends.
  • Use correct tools: Spring compressor, torque wrench, ball joint separator, and alignment equipment.
  • Torque to spec: Never guess â use manufacturer torque settings for all suspension fasteners.
  • Align after work: Any suspension or steering change requires a wheel alignment.
  • Quality used parts only: No leaks, no play, no torn boots, no bent components.
  • Test-drive and document: Low-speed test drive, then record parts used and warranty terms.

Further Reading

  • Bosch Mobility â Chassis and Suspension Systems
  • TyreSafe â Tyre Wear and Safety Guidance
  • Auto Education â Suspension Fundamentals
  • NHTSA â Tyre and Vehicle Safety Resources
  • Bridgestone â Tyre Care and Maintenance

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills programme. Use it alongside hands-on workshop practice and always prioritise safety and customer trust. Your reputation is your most valuable business asset.

quiz.q: What is the bounce test for checking shock absorbers?
options: A) Push down on one corner of the bumper and count bounces
B) Drive over a speed bump and listen for noise
C) Measure the shock's length with a tape
D) Check for oil leaks only
quiz.explanation: If the car bounces more than twice after pushing down, the shock is weak.

quiz.q: Which tool is needed to compress a coil spring when replacing a strut?
quiz.explanation: A spring compressor is essential to safely compress the coil spring on a strut.

quiz.q: What should you check on a used shock absorber from a scrap yard?
options: C) For oil leaks and smooth operation
D) The weight of the shock
quiz.explanation: Oil leaks and uneven resistance indicate a worn shock that should be rejected.

quiz.q: When replacing control arm bushings, how should you tighten the bolts?
options: B) With the suspension loaded (car on ground)
quiz.explanation: Tightening with the suspension loaded prevents bushing twist and premature failure.

quiz.q: What is a sign of worn suspension bushings?
quiz.explanation: Worn bushings allow metal-to-metal contact, causing clunks.

quiz.q: How can you press in a new control arm bushing without a shop press?
options: B) Use a large vice and sockets
quiz.explanation: A vice with suitable sockets can press bushings in evenly.

quiz.q: What should you lubricate polyurethane bushings with?
quiz.explanation: Silicone grease prevents squeaks and doesn't degrade polyurethane.

quiz.q: How do you check for a worn tie rod end?
options: A) Wiggle the tyre at 3 and 9 o'clock
B) Wiggle the tyre at 12 and 6 o'clock
quiz.explanation: Play at 3 and 9 o'clock indicates tie rod end wear.

quiz.q: What tool is used to separate a tie rod end from the steering arm?
quiz.explanation: A pickle fork (ball joint separator) is designed to pop the tapered stud loose.

quiz.q: After replacing a tie rod end, what must you do?
quiz.explanation: Replacing a tie rod end changes toe, so alignment is necessary.

quiz.q: How many turns should you count when unscrewing a tie rod end?
options: C) Count the turns to keep alignment close
quiz.explanation: Counting turns helps maintain approximate alignment before a proper alignment.

quiz.q: What is the correct torque for a tie rod end castle nut?
quiz.explanation: 40-50 Nm is typical for a tie rod end castle nut on many cars.

quiz.q: What is toe-in?
options: A) The front of the tyres pointing inward
B) The front of the tyres pointing outward
quiz.explanation: Toe-in means the front of the tyres are closer together than the rear.

quiz.q: How can you do a basic alignment at home?
options: C) Use a tape measure only
quiz.explanation: A string line parallel to the rear wheel can measure toe.

quiz.q: What is the typical toe-in spec for a Toyota Hilux?
quiz.explanation: Most vehicles specify slight toe-in, often 0-2mm.

quiz.q: After alignment, when should you recheck?
quiz.explanation: Settling can occur, so recheck after 100 km.

quiz.q: What causes centre tread wear on a tyre?
quiz.explanation: Over-inflation causes the centre of the tread to wear faster.

quiz.q: What does feathered edge wear indicate?
quiz.explanation: Feathering is caused by the tyre scrubbing sideways due to incorrect toe.

quiz.q: What does cupped or scalloped tyre wear indicate?
quiz.explanation: Cupping happens when the tyre bounces due to weak damping.

quiz.q: How often should you rotate tyres to even out wear?
quiz.explanation: Regular rotation every 5,000 km promotes even wear.

quiz.q: What should you bring to a scrap yard when looking for suspension parts?
options: A) A torch and pry bar
quiz.explanation: A torch helps inspect in dark areas and a pry bar checks for play.

quiz.q: Which used part should you avoid buying?
options: A) A shock with oil leaks
B) A control arm with good bushings
C) A tie rod with tight ball
D) A strut with good spring
quiz.explanation: Oil leaks indicate a blown shock that will not damp properly.

quiz.q: What should you do with used suspension parts before fitting?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning and painting helps identify cracks and prevents rust.

quiz.q: Why should you replace suspension parts in pairs?
quiz.explanation: Replacing in pairs keeps the suspension balanced left-to-right.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of a clunk when turning the steering wheel?
quiz.explanation: The strut mount bearing often makes noise when turning if worn.

quiz.q: How much can you save buying used suspension parts from a scrap yard?
quiz.explanation: Used parts typically cost 50-70% less than new.

quiz.q: What is the first step when checking uneven tyre wear?
quiz.explanation: Incorrect pressure is a common cause of uneven wear and easy to check first.

quiz.q: What tool can measure tread depth?
quiz.explanation: A gauge, ruler, or coin can all be used to measure tread depth.

quiz.q: When replacing a control arm, what should you do with the ball joint?
options: A) Inspect for play and replace if worn
quiz.explanation: The ball joint is a critical wear point and should be checked.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a sway bar bushing?
options: A) To cushion the sway bar and reduce noise
quiz.explanation: Sway bar bushings isolate the bar from the frame, reducing noise and allowing movement.
